mainTopic: Redeeming a Jew sold to a non-Jew: the lower price, and whether a slave or a walled-city house can be redeemed in parts
overview: The amud opens by finishing a proof that a Jew who sold himself to a non-Jew should be treated strictly, since his sins brought him so low. That proof is pushed back, because the Torah commands that he be redeemed. רב נחמן בר יצחק then shows from two פסוקים, and from the extra word 'בשנים', that he always pays the lower price: the original price if his value rose, his current value if it fell. Next, רב הונא בר חיננא asks רב ששת whether such a slave can be redeemed in parts. רב ששת says no: like a thief who is sold whole, he is redeemed whole. אביי shows that partial redemption can help or hurt, depending on whether the slave's value rises or falls. רב הונא בר חיננא then asks the same question about a house in a walled city. רב ששת answers from רבי שמעון's reasoning that it may be redeemed with borrowed money and in parts. A ברייתא is brought that seems to say the opposite, and the גמרא begins to answer with 'לא קשיא'. The answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the proof: the man was sold to serve idol worship itself
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, quoted as a proof, ends here. Sin can bring a person so low that he is sold to serve עבודה זרה itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the one who is sold to idol worship itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא that was brought to prove we should be strict with a Jew sold to a non-Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes a step-by-step fall caused by sin, and this is the lowest step: being sold to work for עבודה זרה. The point of the proof is that someone who fell this far because of his sins does not deserve an easy redemption price.

keyTerms.meaning: Idol worship
The one who is sold (as a slave)
Itself: serving the idol worship directly, not just a non-Jewish owner

phrases.english: This is the one who is sold to idol worship itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted before this line as a proof for being strict.
steps.raayaObject: That we should be strict about the redemption price of a Jew sold to a non-Jew.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא about how sin leads a person down step by step, until he is sold to עבודה זרה.

steps.title: The Torah itself brings him back: he must be redeemed
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The Torah says not to abandon this person, as דבי רבי ישמעאל teach from the פסוק 'אחרי נמכר גאולה תהיה לו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the verse brought him back. As the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: since this man went and became a priest for idol worship, I might say, 'Let us throw a stone after the one who fell.' So the verse teaches: 'After he is sold, he shall be redeemed; one of his brothers shall redeem him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The other side answers that the Torah itself refuses to give up on this man. It commands that he be redeemed, so the ברייתא is no proof that we should be strict with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have thought a Jew who sank this low should be left alone, like 'throwing a stone after someone who already fell.' The פסוק says the opposite: he must be redeemed. That suggests the Torah wants to help him, not make things harder for him.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse brought him back: the Torah did not give up on him
The school (students) of רבי ישמעאל
A priest of idol worship
Let us throw a stone after the fallen: give up on someone who is already down
Redemption: buying back a slave's freedom

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם, הָא אַהְדְּרֵיהּ קְרָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: There, the verse has brought him back,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the man sold to idol worship in the ברייתא just quoted.

phrases.english: as the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Since this one went
and became a priest for idol worship,
I might say: let us throw a stone after the one who fell.
Therefore the verse teaches:
"After he is sold, he shall be redeemed;
one of his brothers shall redeem him."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:48

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם, הָא אַהְדְּרֵיהּ קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof: the ברייתא cannot show we are strict, because the Torah commands that he be redeemed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof ignores the פסוק that tells us not to abandon him, which shows the Torah's concern for him.

steps.title: Maybe redemption only keeps him from getting lost, but the price can still be strict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. The command to redeem him may only be meant to stop him from blending in among the non-Jews, so the price could still be set strictly because of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say this: 'He shall be redeemed' so that he will not blend in among the non-Jews. But when it comes to the redemption price, let us be strict with him, because of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. It says the duty to redeem him and the question of how much he pays are two separate things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק only proves we must get him out, maybe just to protect him from being lost among the non-Jews. It does not prove we must give him a cheap price. So רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's idea of being strict could still apply to the price.

keyTerms.meaning: To be absorbed or assimilated
Redemption payment: the price paid to free him
We will be strict

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up 'must we redeem him?' with 'how much does he pay?' Everyone agrees he must be redeemed. The only question here is whether the price is set strictly or leniently.

phrases.english: But say: "He shall be redeemed"

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִיטַּמַּע בֵּין הַנׇּכְרִים,
phrases.english: so that he will not be assimilated among the non-Jews;
but regarding the redemption price, let us be strict with him,
based on Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 2 by limiting what the פסוק proves.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 2 that the פסוק 'גאולה תהיה לו' shows the Torah is lenient with him.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק requires redemption only so that he won't assimilate. It says nothing about the price, so the price can still be set strictly.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: two verses are written about this
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק points to two פסוקים about redeeming a Jew from a non-Jew: one speaks of 'many years' and one of 'few years.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Two verses are written. It is written, 'If there are still many years,' and it is written, 'And if only a few years remain.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק starts his answer by setting two פסוקים side by side. He is setting up a question about them that will lead to his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each פסוק gives a different way to figure the price: 'מכסף מקנתו' (from the money he was bought for) and 'כפי שניו' (according to his years). Having two different formulas is what will show that the Torah is lenient on the price itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Two verses are written
Many years (remaining)
Few years remaining

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
Two verses are written.
It is written: "If there are still many years,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:51. The פסוק goes on: he pays back 'from the money he was bought for.'

phrases.english: and it is written: "And if only a few years remain."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:52. That פסוק goes on: 'according to his years.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: תְּרֵי קְרָאֵי כְּתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge of step 3 by bringing פסוקים about the redemption price itself.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New source: verses that deal directly with the price, not only with the duty to redeem.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being lenient was only proven for the duty to redeem him, not for the price.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two verses deal with the price itself, and they will show we are lenient.

steps.title: How can there be both 'many years' and 'few years'?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק asks how the Torah can describe the years as both many and few, so the פסוקים must mean something more than counting years.
steps.simpleTranslation: But are there 'many years' and are there 'few years'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק asks a sharp question about the two פסוקים. It sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוקים were only about counting how many years are left, there would be no need for two separate formulas. The odd wording is a sign that the two פסוקים are really talking about two different situations.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it really so? (opens a question that expects 'no')
Many
Few

phrases.english: But are there many years
and are there few years?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי יֵשׁ שָׁנִים מְרוּבּוֹת וְיֵשׁ שָׁנִים מוּעָטוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the plain meaning of the two פסוקים quoted in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the two different formulas, 'many years' and 'few years', are really teaching.

steps.title: Either way he pays the lower price
steps.stepSummary: If his value went up, he pays 'מכסף מקנתו', the original lower price. If his value went down, he pays 'כפי שניו', his current lower value. Either way the Torah is lenient with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: if his value went up, he pays 'from the money he was bought for.' If his value went down, he pays 'according to his years.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק explains that the two פסוקים cover two cases, and in each case the slave pays the cheaper amount. This answers the challenge from step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because both formulas always give the lower price, the Torah is clearly lenient about the price itself, not only about the duty to redeem him. So רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's idea of being strict does not apply to the redemption price.

keyTerms.meaning: His monetary value went up
His monetary value went down
From the money he was bought for (the original price)
According to his years (his current value)

steps.whatToRemember: A Jew sold to a non-Jew always pays the lower amount to go free. If his value rose, he pays the original price. If his value fell, he pays his current value. The Torah is lenient with him even though he fell so low.
steps.whyThisMatters: This settles the question of the סוגיא: even a Jew sold to a non-Jew, who fell so low because of his sins, still gets the lenient price.

phrases.english: Rather: if his value went up,
he pays "from the money he was bought for";
if his value went down,
he pays "according to his years."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5 and completes the answer to step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two פסוקים cover a rise and a fall in value, and in both cases the slave pays the lower amount.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We are lenient on the redemption price of a Jew sold to a non-Jew.

steps.title: Maybe the verses just count the years left
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that 'many years' and 'few years' simply describe how many years of work are left, not changes in his value.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the Torah means this: if he worked two years and four are left, he pays for four, 'out of the money he was bought for.' If he worked four and two are left, he pays for two, 'according to his years.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's reading. It offers a simpler explanation of the two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5, רב נחמן בר יצחק said 'many' and 'few' cannot both just be counting years. Here the גמרא answers that they can. 'Many' is the case where most of the years are still left, and 'few' is the case where only a few years are left. If so, the פסוקים no longer prove that the Torah is lenient about his value.

keyTerms.meaning: But say, maybe we should explain it this way
This is what it is saying
Remained, were left over
Out of the money he was bought for
According to his years

phrases.english: But say this is what it is saying:
where he served two years
and four remain for him
let him pay him for four, "out of the money he was bought for"
if he served four and two remain for him
let him pay for two, "according to his years"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading given in step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that the פסוקים are about changes in the slave's value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Many' and 'few' can fit simple year-counting: many years left in one case, few in the other.

steps.title: The extra word 'of the years' proves the lenient reading
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah only meant counting years, it would not need the word 'בשנים'. That extra word teaches the rule about his value going up or down.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the פסוק should have said 'if there are yet many years' and 'if few years remain.' Why say 'of the years'? To teach this: if his value went up over the years, he pays 'out of the money he was bought for.' If his value went down over the years, he pays 'according to his years.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the simpler reading. It points to an extra word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'בַּשָּׁנִים' ('of the years') is not needed if the Torah were only counting years. So it must add something new: his value changes over the years. This brings back רב נחמן בר יצחק's rule that he always pays the lower amount.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Let the פסוק write it this way
Of the years, over the years
His value went up
His value went down

steps.whatToRemember: Because of the extra word 'בשנים', a slave sold to a נכרי always pays the lower amount: the original price if his value went up, or his current value if it went down.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse write:
"If there are yet many years"
"If few years remain"
What is "of the years" for?
phrases.notes: The פסוקים literally say 'many of the years' and 'few of the years.' The גמרא is asking about that little extra word.

phrases.english: If his value went up over the years,
he pays "out of the money he was bought for"
If his value went down over the years,
he pays "according to his years."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים only count how many years of work are left.
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra word 'בשנים' shows the Torah is talking about his value changing, and he always pays the lower amount.

steps.title: רב יוסף praises the explanation
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says that רב נחמן בר יצחק explained these פסוקים as clearly as if they had been given at Sinai.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: רב נחמן בר יצחק explained these פסוקים like Sinai.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף ends this discussion by praising רב נחמן בר יצחק's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The praise shows the explanation stands. Every word of the פסוקים now fits, so the reading is accepted as true.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained them, he expounded them
פסוקים
Like Sinai, as if given at הר סיני

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak expounded
these verses like Sinai.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: דַּרְשִׁינְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק לְהָנֵי קְרָאֵי כְּסִינַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Praises the reading confirmed in step 8
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב נחמן בר יצחק's explanation is accepted: the Torah is lenient in pricing the redemption of an עבד עברי sold to a נכרי.

steps.title: Can a slave sold to a non-Jew be redeemed in parts?
steps.stepSummary: After a memory list of the coming topics, רב הונא בר חיננא asks רב ששת whether an עבד עברי sold to a נכרי can pay off part of his price at a time.
steps.simpleTranslation: (Memory list: slave, house, halves, house, slave, relatives.) רב הונא בר חיננא asked רב ששת: a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew, can he be redeemed in parts, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. First it gives a memory list for the coming questions. Then it asks whether the slave can be redeemed bit by bit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Redeeming in parts means paying for some of his years now and the rest later. That would shorten his time with the נכרי. This question sets up the two sides that come next.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid listing the coming topics
He asked him
A Jewish slave
Redeemed in parts, paid off bit by bit

phrases.english: (Mnemonic: slave, house, halves,
phrases.notes: This is a memory list of the topics coming up. Some versions have these words and some don't.

phrases.english: house, slave, relatives).

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chinnana asked of Rav Sheshet:
A Hebrew slave who is sold to a non-Jew,
is he redeemed in parts,
or is he not redeemed in parts?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about the same slave
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an עבד עברי sold to a נכרי can pay part of his price to shorten his time of service.

steps.title: The two sides: compare him to a field, or only when it helps him
steps.stepSummary: One side learns from the shared word 'גאולתו' that, like a שדה אחוזה, he cannot be redeemed in parts. The other side says that comparison may only be used to make things easier for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'His redemption' is said about the slave and 'his redemption' is said about the field, so we learn from the שדה אחוזה. Just as a שדה אחוזה cannot be redeemed in parts, this slave cannot either. Or perhaps we use this comparison only to be lenient, and not to be strict?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out both sides of רב הונא בר חיננא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the same word 'גאולתו' links the slave to the field, so he would follow the field's rule of no partial redemption. Side two: the Torah wants him freed quickly. So the comparison may only be used when it makes things easier for him, and a ban on partial payment would make things harder.

keyTerms.meaning: His or its redemption
An inherited family field
He learns it from, derives it
For a leniency
For a stringency

steps.confusionAlert: This is still a question with two sides. The גמרא has not decided yet.

phrases.english: "His redemption" and "his redemption"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:52 for the slave, and ויקרא 25:26 for the field.

phrases.english: he learns from an ancestral field:

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה אֵינוֹ נִגְאָל לַחֲצָאִין –
phrases.english: just as an ancestral field is not redeemed in parts,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַאי נָמֵי אֵינוֹ נִגְאָל לַחֲצָאִין,
phrases.english: so too this one is not redeemed in parts.
Or perhaps we say it for a leniency,
phrases.notes: He means we compare the slave to the field only when the comparison helps him get free.

phrases.english: but for a stringency we do not say it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two sides of the question asked in step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the shared word 'גאולתו' applies the field's rule against partial redemption to the slave, or only applies when it is lenient for him.

steps.title: רב ששת: Sold as a whole, redeemed as a whole
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת compares the word 'נגאל' to the word 'נמכר' said about a thief. A thief is sold only as a whole person, so the עבד is redeemed only as a whole person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to him: Didn't you say there, about a thief, that 'he is sold' means all of him and not half of him? So too here, 'he is redeemed' means all of him and not half of him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers רב הונא בר חיננא's question. He reminds him of a rule רב הונא בר חיננא already agrees with, and applies it here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About a thief who cannot pay, the תורה says 'ונמכר', and that teaches he is sold only as a whole person. רב ששת reads 'נגאל' the same way. So the עבד cannot be redeemed piece by piece. He goes free only when his whole price is paid.

keyTerms.meaning: He is sold. Said about a thief sold to pay back what he stole
He is redeemed (bought free)
All of him and not half of him
So too, the same here

phrases.english: He said to him: Didn't you say there:
phrases.notes: רב ששת is speaking to רב הונא בר חיננא. 'There' means the case of a thief sold for his theft.

phrases.english: 'He is sold' – all of him and not half of him,
phrases.notes: שמות 22:2

phrases.english: So too, 'he is redeemed' – all of him and not half of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in steps 10-11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can an עבד sold to a נכרי be redeemed in parts?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. Like 'נמכר' by a thief, 'נגאל' means all of him at once.

steps.title: אביי: Partial redemption can help, case one
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the question of partial redemption can make things easier or harder. He first gives the case where it makes things easier: the עבד's value rises after half was paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: If you say he can be redeemed in parts, you will find it can be a leniency or a stringency. A leniency: he was sold for 100, and the redeemer gave 50, half his price. Then he went up in value to 200. If you say he can be redeemed in parts, the redeemer gives 100 and he goes free. If you say he cannot be redeemed in parts, the redeemer gives 150 and he goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains what difference the question really makes. He starts with the case where partial redemption helps the עבד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If parts count, the first 50 already freed half of him. Only the other half is left, and it is now worth 100. If parts do not count, the 50 was only a first payment toward a person now worth 200, so 150 more is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: In halves, in parts
For a leniency and for a stringency
Half of his price
And he went up in value
And he goes out (free)

phrases.english: אביי said: If you say
he is redeemed in parts,
you find it for a leniency and for a stringency.
For a leniency: he sold him for a hundred,
he gave him fifty, half of his price,
and he went up and stood at two hundred,
if you say he is redeemed in parts –
he gives him a hundred and he goes out,
phrases.notes: Half of him is already free, so only the other half (half of 200) is paid.

phrases.english: and if you say he is not redeemed in parts –
he gives him a hundred and fifty and he goes out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר נִגְאָל לַחֲצָאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the practical difference behind the question that רב ששת just answered.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the value rises, partial redemption means a smaller payment (100 instead of 150).

steps.title: But a rise in value doesn't count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. We learned that if his value went up, the redeemer pays by the price he was bought for. So how can the rise to 200 change anything?
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said that if his value went up, we go by 'the money he was bought for'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's first case using a rule we learned earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'מכסף מקנתו' teaches that when the עבד's value rises, the redeemer still pays only the original purchase price. So a rise from 100 to 200 should not matter. אביי's leniency case seems impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: His value went up
From the money he was bought for (ויקרא 25:51)

phrases.english: But you said: if his money (value) increased –
'From the money he was bought for'!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:51

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the leniency case of step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's case where the value rose to 200.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rise in value is ignored ('מכסף מקנתו'), so the price cannot go up to 200.

steps.title: He rose, dropped, and rose again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is one where he was first worth 200, dropped, and then went back up to 200. The rise only brought him back to his original price.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he went up, went down, and went up again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves אביי's case by describing it more exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's case he was bought for 100, but he had been worth 200 at an earlier point. His value dropped and then rose back to 200. Since he is only returning to a value he already had, the rule 'מכסף מקנתו' does not stop the redeemer from paying based on 200.

keyTerms.meaning: That he became more valuable
And he became cheaper

phrases.english: For example, where he went up, and went down, and went up.
phrases.notes: He was first worth 200, then dropped to 100, then climbed back to 200.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The value simply rose above the purchase price, which should not count.
steps.terutzMaskana: The value only returned to the original price of 200, so it counts.

steps.title: אביי: Partial redemption can hurt, case two
steps.stepSummary: אביי gives the case where partial redemption makes things harder: the עבד's value drops after half was paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: You find it for a stringency: he was sold for 200, and the redeemer gave 100, half his price. Then he went down in value to 100. If you say he can be redeemed in parts, the redeemer gives 50 more and he goes free. If you say he cannot be redeemed in parts, those 100 are just a deposit held by the owner. The redeemer gives them to him and he goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his point with the opposite case, where partial redemption costs more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If parts count, half was freed for 100, and the other half is now worth 50, so the total is 150. If parts do not count, the first 100 was only held as a deposit. He is now worth 100 in total, so that 100 covers everything. Here, partial redemption is the harsher view.

keyTerms.meaning: And he dropped in value
A deposit, money held for someone

steps.whatToRemember: Partial redemption helps the עבד when his value rises and hurts him when it falls. רב ששת rules that he is redeemed only all at once.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Leniency' and 'stringency' here describe what happens if you say partial redemption works. It is not a ruling about which view is correct.

phrases.english: You find it for a stringency:
he sold him for two hundred,
he gave a hundred, half of his price,
and he dropped and stood at a hundred,
if you say he is redeemed in parts –
he gives him fifty and he goes out,
and if you say he is not redeemed in parts –
those hundred are a deposit with him,
he gives them to him and he goes out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to אביי's statement after the question and answer of steps 14-15, and gives its second half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the value falls, partial redemption means a larger total payment (150 instead of 100).

steps.title: Can a walled-city house be redeemed in parts?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חיננא asks רב ששת whether a house sold in a walled city can be redeemed in parts. He gives two possible ways to look at it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר חיננא asked רב ששת: If someone sells a house in a walled city, can he buy it back bit by bit, or not? Maybe we learn from the matching word 'its redemption,' which appears both here and by an ancestral field. Just as an ancestral field cannot be redeemed in parts, a house cannot either. Or maybe where the Torah said it, it said it, and where it did not say it, it did not say it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רב הונא בר חיננא asks whether the 'no partial redemption' rule also applies to a house in a walled city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word, 'גאולתו', is written about the field and about the house, so maybe the field's rule carries over to the house. But the Torah spelled out the 'whole redemption' rule only for the field. Maybe it was not meant to carry over.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in walled cities. The seller can buy one back only within the first year after the sale.
Redeemed in halves, meaning bought back bit by bit.
An ancestral field, land inherited in the family.
He learns it, here through a matching word.
Revealed, meaning the Torah spelled it out.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chinnana asked Rav Sheshet:
One who sells a house among the houses of walled cities,
can it be redeemed in halves,
or can it not be redeemed in halves?
Does he learn 'its redemption,' 'its redemption,' from the ancestral field:
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:26 for the field and ויקרא 25:29 for the house.

phrases.aramaic: מָה שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה אֵינָהּ נִגְאֶלֶת לַחֲצָאִין –
phrases.english: just as an ancestral field cannot be redeemed in halves,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הַאי נָמֵי אֵינוֹ נִגְאָל לַחֲצָאִין,
phrases.english: so too this house cannot be redeemed in halves,
or perhaps:
where it revealed, it revealed,
phrases.notes: He means the Torah spelled out the 'whole redemption only' rule for the field.

phrases.english: where it did not reveal, it did not reveal?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from partial redemption of an עבד to partial redemption of a walled-city house, asking רב ששת again.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the field's 'no partial redemption' rule carry over to a walled-city house through the matching word גאולתו?

steps.title: רב ששת answers from רבי שמעון's teaching
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that, according to רבי שמעון's teaching, the house may be redeemed with borrowed money and may be redeemed in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We can learn it from רבי שמעון's teaching. One may borrow money and redeem, and one may redeem in parts. As a ברייתא teaches: 'If he will surely redeem' teaches that one may borrow and redeem, and may redeem in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question. He says the house can be redeemed in parts, and he brings a ברייתא based on רבי שמעון's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doubled wording 'גאל יגאל' is written about someone who consecrated a field (ויקרא 27:19). It is read as giving extra permission: one may use borrowed money and pay in parts. רבי שמעון's reasoning, explained next, is what carries this over to the walled-city house.

keyTerms.meaning: His teaching that learns from the wording of the פסוק.
He borrows money and uses it to redeem.
'If he will surely redeem.' The verb is doubled.

phrases.english: He said to him:
From the teaching of Rabbi Shimon we can learn
that he may borrow and redeem
and may redeem in halves,
as it is taught:
'If he will surely redeem'
phrases.notes: Literally 'redeem, he will redeem.' The doubled word is what the teaching is built on.

phrases.english: teaches that he may borrow and redeem
and may redeem in halves.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מִמִּדְרָשׁוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן נִשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. A walled-city house can be redeemed in parts, and with borrowed money, based on רבי שמעון's reading of the doubled verb.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, a walled-city house can be redeemed in parts and with borrowed money, unlike an ancestral field.

steps.title: רבי שמעון explains why the field's rights are weaker
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון explains his reasoning. The seller of an ancestral field gets it back for free at יובל, so his redemption rights are weaker in other ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: What is the reason? We find that one who sells an ancestral field has a strong position. If יובל arrives and the field was not redeemed, it goes back to its owners at יובל. So his position is weakened in another way: he cannot borrow money to redeem, and he cannot redeem in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון begins giving the reason behind his teaching, starting with the ancestral field. This sets up the contrast with walled-city houses that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah balances the seller's rights. The field seller has a big advantage, because the field returns at יובל anyway. In exchange, he gets stricter redemption rules: no borrowing and no paying in parts.

keyTerms.meaning: His power is strengthened. He has an advantage.
His power is weakened. He has a disadvantage.
The fiftieth year, when sold fields return to their original owners.

steps.confusionAlert: Here the 'weakened power' belongs to the field seller, not the house seller. That is why the field has the strict rules and the house has the lenient ones.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said: What is the reason?
Because we find regarding one who sells an ancestral field
that his power is strengthened,
for if יובל arrives and it was not redeemed,
it returns to its owners at יובל,
so his power is weakened,
in that he may not borrow and redeem
and may not redeem in halves.
phrases.notes: The 'not' from the line before carries over here too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the teaching רב ששת quoted, starting with the field side of the contrast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because the ancestral field returns for free at יובל, its seller may not redeem with borrowed money or in parts.
steps.whyThisMatters: This 'balance of rights' reasoning explains why the field and the house have different redemption rules.

steps.title: The Consecrator Loses More, So He Gets More Options
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון finishes his reasoning. The מקדיש can lose his field to the כהנים at יובל, so the תורה makes his redemption easier: he may borrow and he may redeem in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: But someone who consecrates his field is in a weaker position. If יובל comes and he has not redeemed it, the field goes to the כהנים. To balance that, he is given more power: he may borrow money to redeem it, and he may redeem it in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון gives the second half of his comparison. The person who is מקדיש a field is in the opposite position from the seller in step 19.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19 the seller of a שדה אחוזה gets his field back for free at יובל, so the תורה gives him fewer redemption options. The מקדיש risks losing the field forever to the כהנים, so he gets more options to make up for it. The principle is that a weakness in one area is balanced by a strength in another.

keyTerms.meaning: One who consecrates (gives) his field to the Temple
His position is weakened
His position is strengthened
It goes out to the כהנים, so the owner loses it for good

steps.whyThisMatters: This balancing idea, where one weakness is made up for by one strength, is the whole basis for רב ששת's answer about walled-city houses.

phrases.english: One who consecrates, whose power is weakened,
for if יובל arrives and it was not redeemed,
it goes out to the כהנים at יובל,
his power is strengthened,
in that he may borrow and redeem, and redeem in halves.
phrases.notes: 'In halves' means in parts: he can pay some now and the rest later.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי שמעון's comparison that began in step 19 with the seller of an ancestral field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because the מקדיש can lose his field to the כהנים at יובל, he is allowed to borrow to redeem it and to redeem it in parts.

steps.title: Applying the Logic to a House in a Walled City
steps.stepSummary: The seller of a house in a walled city also has a weak position, since after one full year the house is the buyer's forever. So he too may borrow and redeem in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same goes for someone who sells a house in a walled city. His position is weak, because if a full year passes and he has not redeemed it, the house belongs to the buyer forever. So his position is strengthened: he may borrow to redeem it, and he may redeem it in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת finishes his answer by applying רבי שמעון's principle to the walled-city house that רב הונא בר חיננא asked about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The walled-city house works like the consecrated field. The seller can lose it permanently after one year, just as the מקדיש can lose his field at יובל. Since he has that weakness, he gets the same balancing strength: borrowing and partial redemption are allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in cities that were walled
A full year, the time limit for redeeming such a house
Becomes the buyer's permanently

steps.whatToRemember: Weak position means strong redemption rights. Both the מקדיש and the seller of a walled-city house can lose their property forever, so both may borrow and redeem in parts.

phrases.english: This one who sells a house
among the houses of walled cities, too,
since his power is weakened,
for if a full year passes for him
and it was not redeemed, it becomes the buyer's permanently,
his power is strengthened,
in that he may borrow and redeem, and redeem in halves.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מוֹכֵר בַּיִת בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the principle from steps 19–20 to the walled-city house asked about in step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A seller of a house in a walled city may borrow to redeem it and may redeem it in parts, because he risks losing it permanently after one year.

steps.title: A ברייתא Learns These Rights From a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: A challenge is raised from a ברייתא. It learns from the words 'אם גאל יגאל' that the מקדיש may borrow and redeem in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised an objection: the פסוק says 'If he will surely redeem.' This teaches that he may borrow money to redeem, and that he may redeem in parts.
steps.whatsHappening: A challenge begins. The objector quotes a ברייתא that gets the מקדיש's special rights from a פסוק, not from logic. The full attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same ברייתא רב ששת relied on, but the objector quotes more of it. The rest of the ברייתא, in steps 23–25, will say outright that the seller of a walled-city house may NOT borrow and redeem or redeem in parts. That is the real challenge to רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If he will surely redeem'; the doubled word is used to teach these rights

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
phrases.notes: Someone is now challenging רב ששת's answer from steps 18–21.

phrases.english: "If he will surely redeem"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 27:19

phrases.english: teaches that he may borrow and redeem
and redeem in halves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins quoting the full ברייתא, whose ending (step 25) contradicts רב ששת's answer in steps 18–21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim, based on רבי שמעון, that the walled-city house may be redeemed with borrowed money and in parts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The continuation of this ברייתא (step 25) states that a walled-city house seller may not borrow and redeem or redeem in parts. That directly contradicts רב ששת's answer.

steps.title: Without the פסוק, Logic Would Say the Opposite
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains why the פסוק was needed. A קל וחומר would have taught that the מקדיש may NOT borrow or redeem in parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק was needed because you might have reasoned like this. A seller of an ancestral field is in a strong position, since his field comes back to him at יובל, and still he may not borrow to redeem it or redeem it in parts. A consecrator is in a weak position, since his field goes to the כהנים at יובל. So shouldn't he certainly be unable to borrow or redeem in parts?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. It shows that plain logic, a קל וחומר, would have led to the opposite result. That is why the פסוק had to teach the leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון's reasoning was: weak position, so stronger redemption rights. The ברייתא's קל וחומר runs the other way: if even the person in the strong position cannot borrow or redeem in parts, then the person in the weak position surely cannot. The ברייתא will defend this logic by using the walled-city house as proof (step 25), and that is where the clash with רב ששת comes out.

keyTerms.meaning: For one might have thought
Is it not logical? This opens a קל וחומר
An ancestral field inherited in the family
'Just as', the opening word of a קל וחומר

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the direction of the logic. רבי שמעון said weaker position means more rights. The ברייתא's קל וחומר says weaker position means even fewer rights. The two use the same facts to reach opposite results.
steps.whyThisMatters: Defending this קל וחומר is what leads the ברייתא, in step 25, to state that a walled-city house seller may not borrow or redeem in parts, which clashes with רב ששת.

phrases.english: For one might have thought,
Is it not logical?
Just as one who sells an ancestral field
whose power is strengthened,
for if יובל arrives and it was not redeemed
it returns to its owners at יובל,
and yet his power is weakened,
in that he may not borrow and redeem
or redeem in halves,
then one who consecrates, whose power is weakened,
for if יובל arrives and it was not redeemed
it goes out to the כהנים at יובל,
is it not logical that his power is weakened
in that he may not borrow and redeem, or redeem in halves?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted in step 22 and spells out the קל וחומר that the פסוק had to overturn, which completes the force of the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The balancing logic of רבי שמעון used in steps 19–21.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's קל וחומר treats a weaker position as giving fewer rights, the opposite of רבי שמעון's balancing logic. Defending it will lead to the explicit ruling (step 25) that the walled-city house seller may not borrow or redeem in parts.

steps.title: The ברייתא questions its own קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether the קל וחומר holds up. The seller of a שדה אחוזה is weak because he cannot redeem right away. The מקדיש is strong because he can redeem right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about the seller of an ancestral field? His power is weaker, because he cannot redeem right away. Can you say the same about the מקדיש, whose power is stronger, since he can redeem right away?
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the ברייתא, a challenge is raised against the קל וחומר from step 23. The two cases may not be alike enough to compare.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר said that if the field seller may not borrow or redeem in parts, the מקדיש surely may not. The challenge points to a difference: the field seller must wait before redeeming, but the מקדיש can redeem at once. Since the מקדיש is stronger in this way, maybe he should not be treated more strictly.

keyTerms.meaning: An ancestral field, inherited land of the family
His power is weakened, he is in a worse position
His power is strengthened, he is in a better position
To redeem immediately
One who dedicates his field to הקדש

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is still part of the ברייתא itself. The ברייתא is testing its own קל וחומר before it explains why the פסוק was needed.

phrases.english: What about one who sells an ancestral field,
whose power is weakened
to redeem it immediately,
will you say the same about one who consecrates his field,
whose power is strengthened to redeem it immediately?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the קל וחומר given in step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The קל וחומר comparing the field seller to the מקדיש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The field seller is weaker because he cannot redeem right away. The מקדיש is stronger, so a stringency on the field seller cannot simply be carried over to him.

steps.title: The walled-city house proves otherwise, and this clashes with the earlier ruling
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers with the house in a walled city. That seller can also redeem right away, yet he may not borrow or redeem in parts. This contradicts step 21.
steps.simpleTranslation: The seller of a house in a walled city will prove the point. He can redeem right away, and still he may not borrow to redeem or redeem in parts!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא saves its קל וחומר by bringing the walled-city house as proof. The ברייתא's wording also contradicts what was said earlier, and that is the real challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being able to redeem right away does not lead to more lenient rules, because the walled-city house seller can do so and still may not borrow or redeem in parts. So the קל וחומר stands. The ברייתא says plainly that this house seller may NOT borrow or redeem in parts, but step 21 said he MAY.

keyTerms.meaning: Houses in cities surrounded by a wall
Will prove, a counter-example that breaks the objection
Borrowing money in order to redeem
Redeeming in parts, little by little

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main contradiction of the section. The גמרא must now explain how the walled-city house seller can both may and may not borrow or redeem in parts.

phrases.english: One who sells a house among the houses of walled cities
will prove it,
since his power is strengthened to redeem immediately
and yet he may not borrow and redeem
nor redeem in parts!
phrases.notes: This is the problem: back in step 21 we said this seller MAY borrow and redeem in parts.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹכֵר בַּיִת בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה יוֹכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 24 within the ברייתא, and in doing so completes the challenge against step 21
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in step 21 that the walled-city house seller may borrow and redeem in parts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא clearly states that the walled-city house seller may not borrow or redeem in parts, which directly contradicts step 21.

steps.title: The גמרא begins its answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the contradiction is not a real difficulty. The explanation follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its answer to the contradiction. It announces there is no real problem, and the explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא קשיא' tells us the two sources will be shown to be talking about different things. The details of how they fit together are given in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult, the opening of an answer that reconciles two sources

phrases.english: It is not difficult:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the answer to the contradiction raised in step 25
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and step 21 seem to give opposite rulings on the walled-city house seller.
steps.terutzMaskana: The גמרא will show that the two sources do not truly conflict. The details come in the following lines.
